source.title: Labeling Neural Representations with Inverse Recognition
source.authors: Kirill Bykov; Laura Kopf; Shinichi Nakajima; Marius Kloft; M. Höhne

record.tranche_reason: The paper studies labeling neural representations in vision models, but it does not test the stated neuron-pole shares, the listed language-model claims, or explanation performance on held-out activating examples.
record.gate_note: The paper reports adjacent results on labeling vision-model representations. Table 1's explanation-accuracy comparisons are recorded as related findings, not as tests of the claim versions. Other reported AUC, IoU, and classification results evaluate INVERT or related tasks and do not measure any version's stated outcome.
record.test_reason: This is a method paper proposing INVERT, an AUC-based labeling method for vision-model neurons. Its only reference to the claim's sources is a citation of Bills et al. in related work. It reports no share of interpretable or monosemantic neurons, no language-model results, no test of the cat-and-car neuron and no held-out simulation scoring. Table 1 measures how accurately each labeling tool recovers known labels of output neurons, not how interpretable a model's neurons are. That is the tool's own performance, so the study does not test any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that INVERT links neurons to compositional concepts with an AUC metric and a significance test. They say it helps audit spurious correlations and explain circuits, but still needs labeled data.
record.recipe_differences: INVERT uses labeled image datasets and AUC to select compositional concepts for vision-model representations. It is not the Qwen neuron-pole audit or an evaluation of language-model explanations on held-out text.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that explanation AUC and concept fraction vary with formula length and the minimum concept-fraction parameter α.

fits_no_version.finding: On output neurons with known labels, INVERT recovers the correct class more often than NetDissect (e.g. GoogleNet 82.2% vs 19.7%; Table 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Label-recovery accuracy of vision neuron-labeling tools depends strongly on the tool, for output neurons whose labels are known.

fits_no_version.finding: For 50 sampled feature-extractor neurons per model, the highest-AUC explanations are usually a single narrow ImageNet class. Broader explanations lower AUC, a trade-off the authors call simplicity-precision (Fig. 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In ImageNet vision models, broader concept labels for hidden neurons come at a cost in AUC compared with narrow single-class labels.

record.problems: The method depends on labeled data. The reported explanation-accuracy comparison uses supervised vision models with known ground-truth labels and does not establish the claim's language-model or held-out-explanation outcomes.
record.rows_left_out: Other AUC and IoU metric comparisons, random-explanation checks, and downstream classification results were omitted because they do not measure any claim version; see Sections 4.1–4.2, 5.3, and Appendices A.5–A.7.

untested.parts: All: no Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit or job shares.
All: no language models, no dense versus mixture-of-experts comparison, no scaling.
All: InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron and the pose or recursive-generalization account are not examined.
Share of interpretable hidden neurons, and its dependence on architecture, regularization or tools. Only tool accuracy on output neurons is reported.
All: circuits in ResNet18 are shown only qualitatively, with no attribution graphs in large models and no reconstruction-error comparison.
All: no test of whether explanations from activating examples predict firing elsewhere.
All: no simulation-based scoring of language-model neurons.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'discusses' is changed to 'cites_only': the paper only cites Bills et al. and never engages the claim. All rows are tool-versus-tool accuracies, which are selection or method-performance values rather than measures of any version.

versions.untested_parts: Qwen3-32B neuron-pole proportions and the fractions with one job, two related jobs, or not-yet-understood jobs.
Cross-model shares, dense versus mixture-of-experts comparisons, and scaling up to trillions of parameters.
The InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron and the proposed pose or recursive-generalization account.
Whether architecture, regularization, or tool quality explains messy neurons, and the claimed change in interpretable-neuron share from about 5% to about 99%.
Attribution graphs built from a large model's own neurons and whether they explain behavior without a trained replacement model or reconstruction error.
Whether explanations fitted to activating examples predict firing on separate examples.
Automated simulation-based scoring of language-model neuron explanations on new text, including the share with good scores.

relation.reason: Bills et al. [35] appears only in a related-work citation list on mechanistic interpretability in NLP (refs 32-35). The paper never mentions polysemanticity or superposition and never discusses the claim.

tranche.reason: INVERT is a labeling method for vision-model neurons. It reports no share of interpretable or monosemantic neurons and has no language-model results. Its Table 1 measures how well the tool recovers the known labels of output neurons, not how many hidden neurons are clean. It neither tests the claim nor uses it as a tool.

source_check.notes: All 10 rows match Table 1 cell for cell. They compare the study's own tool with NetDissect at recovering ground-truth labels of output logit neurons. That is tool accuracy, not a share of interpretable neurons, so it does not bear on V4. The rows arguably should not be rows. There are no verdicts and none are warranted.
